chapter: The State: Meaning and Essential Elements
trick: Four elements and no more: population, territory, government, sovereignty. Drop sovereignty and you have a state within a state — West Bengal is not a state in political science, because it does not possess sovereignty. That distinction is the single most tested point in the chapter.

video.query: elements of state population territory government sovereignty class 11 political science

data.prompt: Which of these is NOT an essential element of the state?
data.because: The four essential elements are population, territory, government and sovereignty. A written constitution is not required — the United Kingdom is a state without one.

chapter: Theories of the Origin of the State
trick: Five explanations of where the state came from, and only one is accepted today. Divine origin says God made it, force says the strong seized it, patriarchal and matriarchal say the family grew into it, social contract says people agreed to it — and the evolutionary theory says all of these worked together over time, which is why it is the accepted view.

video.query: theories of origin of state divine force social contract evolutionary class 11

data.prompt: Match each theory of the state's origin with what it claims.

pairs.right: The state was created by God and the ruler answers only to Him
The state arose when the strong subdued the weak — 'war begat the king'
The state grew out of the family, tracing descent through the father — Sir Henry Maine
The earliest families traced descent through the mother — McLennan and Morgan
The state was deliberately created by an agreement among people
The state grew slowly out of kinship, religion, force, property and political consciousness — the accepted view

chapter: Social Contract Theory: Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau
trick: All three start in a state of nature and all three end with a contract, but they disagree about what that state was like — and that disagreement decides everything after it. Hobbes: nasty, brutish and short, so surrender everything to an absolute sovereign. Locke: mostly peaceful but insecure, so surrender only some rights, and rebel if the trust is broken. Rousseau: happy and free, so obey only the General Will.

video.query: hobbes locke rousseau social contract state of nature class 11 political science

data.prompt: Which contract theorist does each position belong to?

items.label: The state of nature was 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short'
Men were born free but are everywhere in chains

Wrote Leviathan and defended absolute sovereignty

Individuals surrendered all rights except the right to life
Held to be the philosopher of the Glorious Revolution and of limited government
Inspired the French Revolution and popular sovereignty

trick: Sovereignty is the supreme power of the state, and its characteristics are absoluteness, permanence, universality, inalienability and indivisibility. The last one is the trap: sovereignty may be divided in its exercise between centre and states, but in theory it cannot be divided and still be sovereignty.

data.prompt: Match each characteristic or kind of sovereignty with its meaning.

pairs.right: No legal power stands above the sovereign inside the state
Sovereignty lasts as long as the state; governments come and go
It extends over every person and association within the territory
It cannot be given away without destroying the state
There can be only one sovereign power in a state
The authority recognised by law as supreme lawmaker
The body of citizens behind the legal sovereign — the electorate
Power actually obeyed, whether or not it is lawful

chapter: Theories of Sovereignty: Monistic and Pluralist
trick: Monism says there is one sovereign, supreme over every association — Austin's position. Pluralism says the state is one association among many, and the church, the trade union and the family have authority of their own — Laski's position. The exam asks you to name which camp a sentence comes from, so tie each name to its camp.

video.query: monistic and pluralistic theory of sovereignty austin laski class 11

data.prompt: Sort each statement into the theory of sovereignty it belongs to.

items.label: Law is the command of the determinate superior
The state is only one of many associations serving human needs
Sovereignty is indivisible and cannot be shared
Authority should be distributed among churches, unions and local bodies
The sovereign's power is legally unlimited
The state earns obedience by service, not by command

chapter: Political Thinkers: Aristotle, Austin and Laski
trick: One line each and the three are fixed. Aristotle: man is by nature a political animal, and the state exists for the good life — he is the father of political science. Austin: sovereignty is the command of a determinate superior. Laski: liberty and the state are not opposites, and the state must justify itself by what it does for people.

Pluralism; the state is one association among many and must earn obedience
The classification of governments into monarchy, aristocracy and polity, and their perversions
A definite person or body whose commands are habitually obeyed and who obeys no one
Liberty is the absence of restraint on those conditions that make for a full life
